name: 10. Launch and post-launch
description: Go-live checklist, support model, feedback loop, analytics, versioning.

cards.subject: The production secrets check
says: confirms credentials are set for the live environment
confirms no key or password is committed to the repository
cards.use: want to be sure keys cannot leak through source control
not: is satisfied when the repository is private, so live passwords may be committed

cards.subject: The backup restore test
says: proves a backup can actually be restored
turns a backup from an assumption into a tested fact
cards.use: need to trust your backup before a risky change
not: is passed as soon as the nightly backup job reports success

cards.subject: The migration dry run
says: applies the schema change to a copy of production data first
reveals locking and duration problems before launch day
cards.use: need to know how long a database change will take on real volumes
not: proves the backup can be restored

cards.subject: The HTTPS and security headers check
says: confirms the site is served over TLS with a valid certificate
confirms headers such as HSTS and a content security policy are present
cards.use: want to verify transport security on the live domain
not: is unnecessary when the hosting provider advertises security

cards.subject: The sign-up control check
says: confirms registration is open, closed or invite-only as intended
stops unknown people creating accounts on day one
cards.use: launch to a limited audience first
not: is only needed for public consumer products

cards.subject: The rollback readiness check
says: confirms a known way back exists before release
includes knowing the previous version can still be deployed
cards.use: want proof that a bad release can be undone quickly
not: is complete once the team agrees to fix forward if anything breaks

cards.subject: The monitoring and alert check
says: confirms alerts reach a person before launch
includes a test alert that is actually received
cards.use: want to be told about failures before users report them
not: is complete once dashboards exist, even if nobody is paged

cards.subject: The smoke test on production
says: runs a few critical user paths against the live system after deployment
is quick enough to repeat on every release
cards.use: have just deployed and need fast evidence the core paths work
not: replaces the full regression suite

cards.subject: The go/no-go meeting
says: collects a named yes or no from each accountable owner
ends with a recorded decision and the gaps accepted
cards.use: need a deliberate launch decision rather than drift into release
not: is a formality held after the release has already started

cards.subject: The DNS and certificate lead-time check
says: confirms DNS changes were made early enough to propagate
confirms certificates are issued and not close to expiry
cards.use: plan a cut-over to a new domain or host
not: can be done in the final minutes before launch because changes take effect at once

cards.subject: The known-gap register
says: lists open issues accepted for launch with an owner and date
keeps accepted risk visible instead of hidden
cards.use: must launch with some problems still open
not: is a list of defects the team hopes nobody will read

cards.subject: Exit criteria
says: state measurable conditions that must be true to release
are agreed before testing starts
cards.use: want to avoid arguing about whether the product is ready
not: are written after testing, once the results are known

cards.subject: The definition of done
says: is a shared checklist a single work item must satisfy
applies to every item, not just the release
cards.use: need a consistent bar for finished work in the team
not: describes when the whole release can ship

cards.subject: A release candidate
says: is a build intended to ship unless a blocking defect is found
is the exact artefact that was tested
cards.use: want to promote the same build through environments
not: is rebuilt from source separately for each environment

cards.subject: A code freeze
says: stops non-essential changes entering the release branch
is followed only by agreed fixes for blocking issues
cards.use: need a stable build for final testing
not: stops all work in the team until release day

cards.subject: A regression suite pass
says: shows previously working behaviour still works
is run against the release candidate
cards.use: want to catch breakage caused by new changes
not: proves that new features meet their requirements

cards.subject: A performance baseline
says: records response times and resource use before the change
lets a later measurement be judged better or worse
cards.use: need to know whether the release made the system slower
not: is a fixed target agreed with the customer

cards.subject: A load test at expected peak
says: exercises the system at the traffic it is forecast to meet
exposes bottlenecks that functional tests cannot
cards.use: expect a launch day traffic spike
not: proves the system will survive any amount of traffic

cards.subject: A security sign-off
says: records that a named person reviewed the known risks
is evidence for an auditor of who accepted what
cards.use: need an accountable approval for launching a system holding personal data
not: guarantees the system has no vulnerabilities

cards.subject: A readiness review
says: weighs open defects and risks against agreed exit criteria
includes operations and support, not just developers
cards.use: want a cross-functional view before committing to a date
not: is run by developers alone because only they know the code

cards.subject: Drafted release notes
says: describe what changed in language users understand
are ready before the release, not after
cards.use: want users and support to know what is new
not: are produced from commit messages without editing

cards.subject: A rollback
says: returns the system to the previously released version
is only quick when it was prepared and rehearsed
cards.use: need to undo a release within minutes
not: is always possible whatever data migrations ran

cards.subject: A roll forward
says: ships a new fix instead of reverting
is the usual answer once a destructive migration has run
cards.use: cannot revert because the data has already changed shape
not: is faster than a rollback in every case

cards.subject: A blue-green deployment
says: keeps two full production environments and switches traffic between them
makes rollback a traffic switch back
cards.use: want near-instant rollback and can afford duplicate infrastructure
not: releases to a small share of users first

cards.subject: A canary release
says: sends a small share of traffic to the new version first
compares health of the new version against the old before widening
cards.use: want real traffic evidence before exposing everyone
not: keeps a full idle copy of production waiting

cards.subject: A rolling deployment
says: replaces instances one batch at a time
keeps old and new versions running together for a while
cards.use: must update a fleet without downtime and without duplicate infrastructure
not: switches all traffic in a single step

cards.subject: A feature flag
says: turns a feature on or off without a new deployment
separates deploying code from releasing it
cards.use: want to release a feature to a chosen group or switch it off quickly
not: is removed automatically once the feature is released

cards.subject: A kill switch
says: disables one risky capability instantly
is built before launch and tested
cards.use: expect one dependency or feature may need to be shut off in an emergency
not: is a flag that is added after an incident

cards.subject: A dark launch
says: runs new code on real traffic without showing results to users
validates behaviour and load before release
cards.use: want to test a new component under production load invisibly
not: announces the feature only to internal staff

cards.subject: A big-bang release
says: switches every user to the new version at once
concentrates all the risk in one moment
cards.use: cannot run old and new versions side by side
not: is the lowest-risk release strategy

cards.subject: The expand-contract migration pattern
says: adds new schema alongside the old before removing the old
lets old and new code run against the same database
cards.use: need a database change that stays rollback-safe
not: drops the old column in the same release that stops using it

cards.subject: A point of no return
says: is the step after which rollback is no longer possible
should be identified and decided on purpose before release
cards.use: plan a release containing an irreversible data change
not: exists only in very large projects

cards.subject: A launch communication plan
says: says who is told what, through which channel and when
covers internal staff as well as users
cards.use: want a launch with no surprises for stakeholders
not: is written after launch, once outcomes are known

cards.subject: A stakeholder update
says: gives sponsors a short status, risks and next steps
is sent on an agreed cadence
cards.use: need to keep sponsors informed without meetings
not: lists every task completed

cards.subject: A status page
says: shows the current health of the service to users
is hosted separately from the service it reports on
cards.use: want users to check for an outage without contacting support
not: reports only planned maintenance

cards.subject: A maintenance window notice
says: warns users of planned downtime in advance
states when it starts, how long it lasts and what is affected
cards.use: plan a deliberate interruption of the service
not: is sent after the maintenance has started

cards.subject: An internal enablement briefing
says: prepares support and sales staff before users see the change
gives them answers to the likely questions
cards.use: want front-line staff to hear about a launch before customers do
not: is sent to users the day of release

cards.subject: An incident communication cadence
says: promises the next update time even when there is nothing new
reduces the stream of repeat questions during an outage
cards.use: are in the middle of an incident and users are asking for news
not: sends an update only when the cause is known

cards.subject: A holding statement
says: acknowledges a problem before the cause is known
avoids guessing or blaming
cards.use: need to respond quickly to a public problem that is not yet understood
not: waits until the root cause is confirmed

cards.subject: A customer migration guide
says: walks users through the steps needed to move to the new version
states clearly what they must do and by when
cards.use: release a change that users must act on
not: only lists new features

cards.subject: A deprecation notice
says: announces that a feature will be removed at a stated date
gives a replacement and a timetable
cards.use: plan to retire something users depend on
not: removes the feature immediately but explains why

cards.subject: Staged announcement timing
says: tells internal teams first, then customers, then the public
matches the announcement to when the rollout reaches each audience
cards.use: are rolling out in stages and do not want to promise what users cannot yet use
not: announces to everyone at the start of the rollout

cards.subject: A support tier
says: is a level of help with a defined scope and skill
passes problems up when it cannot solve them
cards.use: need to decide who handles which questions
not: means a customer pays for a higher grade of service

cards.subject: First-line support
says: answers how-to questions and applies known fixes from documentation
logs and routes everything it cannot resolve
cards.use: want routine questions handled without engineers
not: changes code and infrastructure to fix faults

cards.subject: Second-line support
says: investigates faults by reading logs and reproducing issues
can make small configuration changes
cards.use: have a problem the documentation does not cover
not: is limited to reading from a script

cards.subject: An escalation path
says: names who to contact next and after how long
ends at someone who can change code or infrastructure
cards.use: want a stuck problem to reach a decision maker
not: is improvised during each incident

cards.subject: A severity level
says: classifies an issue by its impact on users and the business
sets how quickly the response must start
cards.use: need to decide whether a problem wakes someone at night
not: is chosen by whoever reports the problem

cards.subject: A service level agreement
says: is a stated commitment on response or availability
carries consequences if it is missed
cards.use: are promising users a target for response
not: should be set to the best result ever achieved

cards.subject: A response target versus a resolution target
says: measures time to first meaningful reply, not time to fix
can be met even when the problem takes days to solve
cards.use: are writing support targets and must not promise a fix time you cannot control
not: are two names for the same measure

cards.subject: A runbook
says: gives step-by-step instructions for a known task or incident
is written so a tired person can follow it at night
cards.use: want an incident handled the same way by anyone on call
not: describes the design of the system

cards.subject: A knowledge base article
says: answers one recurring question in plain language
lets users solve a problem without contacting support
cards.use: see the same question arrive repeatedly
not: is private to the engineering team

cards.subject: An on-call rotation
says: shares out-of-hours responsibility among named people
needs a handover and a fair limit on load
cards.use: must have somebody reachable for urgent problems outside office hours
not: makes one person permanently responsible

cards.subject: Triage
says: sorts incoming issues by impact and urgency
assigns an owner before work begins
cards.use: face a queue of mixed reports after launch
not: fixes issues in the order they arrived

cards.subject: Follow-the-sun support
says: hands support between teams in different time zones
needs a precise handover note at each shift change
cards.use: need near round-the-clock cover without night shifts
not: relies on one team working all night

cards.subject: An uptime check
says: tests from outside whether the service responds
tells you the service is down, not why
cards.use: want a basic signal that the service is reachable
not: replaces logs and metrics

cards.subject: A dashboard
says: shows chosen health measures in one place
is for looking, not for being woken
cards.use: need an at-a-glance view during a launch
not: is a substitute for alerts

cards.subject: An error rate
says: measures the share of requests that fail
rises when something is broken for users
cards.use: want one number that reflects user-visible failure
not: measures how slow responses are

cards.subject: A latency percentile
says: reports the response time that a given share of requests beat
shows slow experiences that an average hides
cards.use: want to see the worst experiences, not the average
not: is the average response time

cards.subject: Log aggregation
says: collects logs from many servers into one searchable place
speeds up finding the cause of a fault
cards.use: need to search logs across several machines during an incident
not: stores only the errors

cards.subject: The four golden signals
says: are latency, traffic, errors and saturation
give a compact first view of any service
cards.use: need a starting set of measures for a new service
not: are CPU, memory, disk and network

cards.subject: A service level indicator
says: is a measured quantity describing service behaviour
feeds a target such as an objective
cards.use: need a precise measure of how well the service is working
not: is the promise made to the customer

cards.subject: A service level objective
says: is an internal target for an indicator over a period
is looser than a contract and tighter than aspiration
cards.use: want a clear goal for reliability
not: is the contract with penalty clauses

cards.subject: An error budget
says: is the amount of unreliability an objective allows
guides how much risky change the team may ship
cards.use: must decide whether to pause releases to improve stability
not: is the money allocated to fixing bugs

cards.subject: Synthetic monitoring
says: runs scripted user journeys on a schedule
detects failures even when no real users are present
cards.use: want to know a key journey works at 3 a.m.
not: measures what real users actually experienced

cards.subject: Real user monitoring
says: records the experience of actual visitors in their browsers
shows differences by device and location
cards.use: want to see performance as customers really experience it
not: runs scripted journeys on a schedule

cards.subject: Symptom-based alerting
says: pages on what users experience rather than on internal causes
reduces noisy alerts that need no action
cards.use: want alerts that matter
not: pages whenever any resource passes a threshold

cards.subject: Alert fatigue
says: builds when too many alerts need no action
leads people to ignore the one that matters
cards.use: notice on-call staff are muting notifications
not: is cured by adding more alerts

cards.subject: Distributed tracing
says: follows one request across several services
shows where the time is spent
cards.use: need to find which service in a chain is slow
not: counts the requests a single service handles

cards.subject: A feedback loop
says: collects signals, decides what they mean, makes a change and checks the effect
is repeated on a schedule
cards.use: want shipping to lead to learning
not: ends when the product is released

cards.subject: A qualitative signal
says: explains why users behave as they do
comes from interviews, comments and support questions
cards.use: need the reason behind a number
not: tells you how many users did something

cards.subject: A quantitative signal
says: counts what happened and how often
comes from analytics events and error rates
cards.use: need to know how many users reached a step
not: explains the motivation behind a decision

cards.subject: An analytics event
says: records one user action with a name and properties
should answer a question decided in advance
cards.use: want to measure a specific behaviour
not: should be added for everything just in case

cards.subject: A funnel
says: shows how many users drop at each step of a journey
highlights the step to fix first
cards.use: want to find where sign-ups are lost
not: groups users by when they joined

cards.subject: A cohort
says: groups users who share a starting point such as sign-up week
lets behaviour be compared over time
cards.use: want to know whether newer users behave better than older ones
not: shows steps in a journey

cards.subject: Retention
says: measures the share of users who come back after a period
is a stronger sign of value than sign-ups
cards.use: want evidence that people keep using the product
not: counts the total number of registrations

cards.subject: An activation metric
says: marks the point where a new user first gets real value
is a better early signal than registration
cards.use: need to know whether new users are reaching the point of value
not: counts the people who saw the landing page

cards.subject: A vanity metric
says: looks impressive but does not guide a decision
tends to rise whatever the team does
cards.use: are shown a large number that no action depends on
not: is always a poor choice in every case

cards.subject: An A/B test
says: compares two variants on randomly split users
needs enough users and time to separate effect from noise
cards.use: want to know whether a change caused an improvement
not: compares behaviour before and after release only

cards.subject: A novelty effect
says: inflates a metric briefly because a change is new
fades as users get used to it
cards.use: see a spike right after a redesign and want to know if it will last
not: means the change was clearly a success

cards.subject: A guardrail metric
says: watches for harm while another metric is optimised
stops a win in one area hiding a loss elsewhere
cards.use: are running an experiment on conversion and must not hurt speed or errors
not: is the main goal of an experiment

cards.subject: Data minimisation
says: collects only the data needed for the stated purpose
keeps emails and secrets out of event names and URLs
cards.use: design analytics for a product holding personal data
not: collects everything now in case it becomes useful

cards.subject: First-party data
says: is data your own product already records
needs no third-party tracker
cards.use: want completion or score trends from your own database
not: is bought from an external provider

cards.subject: Closing the loop with users
says: tells users what was fixed after they raised it
encourages more feedback
cards.use: want people to keep reporting problems
not: means the feedback request is closed without reply

cards.subject: An in-product survey
says: asks a short question at the moment of use
has a higher response rate than a long email survey
cards.use: want fresh opinion about one feature
not: replaces user interviews

cards.subject: Semantic versioning
says: uses a MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH number
signals the kind of change through which part increases
cards.use: want users to judge upgrade risk from the number
not: increases by one for every release regardless of change

cards.subject: A patch version
says: increases for backward-compatible bug fixes
does not add features
cards.use: ship only a bug fix
not: is for breaking changes

cards.subject: A minor version
says: increases for backward-compatible new features
resets the patch number to zero
cards.use: add a feature without breaking existing users
not: is for breaking changes

cards.subject: A major version
says: increases when a change breaks backward compatibility
resets the minor and patch numbers to zero
cards.use: ship a change that existing users must adapt to
not: is raised for every large feature, compatible or not

cards.subject: Zero-based versions
says: signal that the interface may still change
give no compatibility promise between minors
cards.use: are building early software with a 0.x number
not: mean the software is unusable

cards.subject: A pre-release tag
says: marks a version as not yet final, such as -rc.1
sorts before the release it leads to
cards.use: want to publish a build for testing
not: sorts after the final release

cards.subject: Calendar versioning
says: builds the number from the release date
suits products where time matters more than compatibility
cards.use: ship on a schedule and no compatibility promise is needed
not: is another name for semantic versioning

cards.subject: A Git tag
says: names a specific commit permanently
lets you find exactly what was deployed
cards.use: need to point at the code of release 1.2.0
not: moves forward automatically with each commit

cards.subject: A changelog
says: lists notable changes per version
is written for people, not generated from every commit
cards.use: want users to see what changed between releases
not: is a copy of the commit log

cards.subject: A conventional commit
says: puts a type such as fix or feat at the start of the message
lets tools derive the version bump and changelog
cards.use: want release notes and versions generated from history
not: is any commit message that is short

cards.subject: A breaking change
says: forces existing users to change their code or data
should raise the major version
cards.use: remove or rename something others rely on
not: is safe to ship in a patch release

cards.subject: A lockfile
says: records the exact versions of dependencies installed
makes builds repeatable
cards.use: need the same dependencies on every machine
not: upgrades dependencies automatically on each install

cards.subject: API versioning
says: lets old clients keep working while new ones adopt changes
needs a published period before an old version is retired
cards.use: must change an interface used by clients you do not control
not: lets you change responses silently as long as the URL stays the same

cards.subject: Hypercare
says: is a period of intensified support right after launch
has a defined end
cards.use: expect a rush of issues after go-live
not: continues indefinitely at the same staffing level

cards.subject: Hypercare exit criteria
says: state when normal support can take over
include stable metrics and few open high-severity issues
cards.use: need to decide when the extra support can stop
not: are met when the calendar period passes

cards.subject: A war room
says: gathers the people needed to resolve issues quickly during launch
has a named lead and a log of decisions
cards.use: expect a complex launch needing fast cross-team decisions
not: replaces the on-call rotation permanently

cards.subject: A handover
says: moves responsibility from one team to another
is complete only when the receiver accepts it
cards.use: pass a finished system to the team that will run it
not: is complete when the document is emailed

cards.subject: A handover pack
says: bundles documentation, access, contacts and known issues
gives the receiver what they need to operate the system
cards.use: are transferring a system to operations
not: contains only the source code

cards.subject: A knowledge transfer session
says: has the builders explain how the system works and fails
is best recorded and paired with documents
cards.use: want operations to learn from the people who built it
not: can replace written documentation

cards.subject: Shadowing
says: lets the receiving team watch the builders operate
comes before the receiving team takes the lead
cards.use: start a handover
not: has the receivers lead while builders watch

cards.subject: Reverse shadowing
says: has the receiving team operate while builders observe
lets mistakes be caught safely before the final handover
cards.use: want to confirm the receivers can run it unaided
not: has the builders operate while receivers watch

cards.subject: A named service owner
says: is one accountable person for a live service
answers for its availability and roadmap
cards.use: need clarity on who decides about a service
not: is a team mailbox with no specific person

cards.subject: Operational acceptance
says: confirms the operating team agrees it can support the system
is based on agreed criteria
cards.use: want operations to be able to refuse an unready handover
not: is a signature collected after the system is already live

cards.subject: A warranty period
says: is a period when the builder fixes defects at no extra cost
has an agreed length and scope
cards.use: hand over a delivered system from a supplier
not: covers all new feature requests

cards.subject: A retrospective
says: is a regular team review of how the work went
ends with a small number of agreed improvements
cards.use: want the team to improve how it works
not: is used to assess individuals' performance

cards.subject: A blameless post-incident review
says: focuses on how the system and process allowed the failure
asks what made the action sensible at the time
cards.use: want honest accounts after an outage
not: names the person who caused the failure

cards.subject: Timeline reconstruction
says: builds a minute-by-minute record of what happened
is based on logs and chat history, not memory
cards.use: start an incident review
not: records only the final root cause

cards.subject: Contributing factors
says: are the several conditions that together allowed an incident
replace the search for one root cause
cards.use: find that an incident had no single trigger
not: name the one person to retrain

cards.subject: An action item with an owner and date
says: turns discussion into a task someone is accountable for
is tracked until finished
cards.use: want a retrospective to change something
not: is satisfied by agreeing that the team will try harder

cards.subject: The five whys
says: asks why repeatedly to move from symptom towards cause
can mislead if it follows a single line of reasoning
cards.use: want a quick way to dig into a problem
not: guarantees one true root cause

cards.subject: Start, stop, continue
says: asks what to begin, end and keep doing
gives a simple structure for a retrospective
cards.use: want a lightweight retrospective format
not: is a post-incident report template

cards.subject: A launch metrics review
says: compares results against the targets set before launch
feeds the next prioritisation
cards.use: need to know whether the launch achieved its aim
not: lists the tasks that were completed

cards.subject: A benefits realisation review
says: checks months later that expected benefits were delivered
is held after the project team has moved on
cards.use: must show whether an investment paid off
not: is performed on launch day

cards.subject: Unactioned retrospective items
says: erode trust in the process
make people stop contributing
cards.use: see the same retrospective points raised in several sessions
not: show that the team is improving

cards.subject: Corrective maintenance
says: fixes defects found after release
responds to problems reported by users
cards.use: need to repair a fault in live software
not: adds new capability

cards.subject: Adaptive maintenance
says: changes software to suit a changed environment
covers new operating system or platform versions
cards.use: must keep software working after its platform changes
not: fixes a fault found by a user

cards.subject: Perfective maintenance
says: improves performance or usability of working software
adds enhancements users ask for
cards.use: want to improve software that is not broken
not: avoids future faults before they appear

cards.subject: Preventive maintenance
says: restructures code to avoid future faults
reduces the risk of later problems
cards.use: want to lower future cost by cleaning up before it breaks
not: repairs faults users have reported

cards.subject: Technical debt
says: is the extra future cost created by shortcuts taken now
accrues interest as the shortcuts spread
cards.use: decided to ship fast knowing the code needed rework
not: is a measure of how much money was borrowed

cards.subject: A dependency update
says: brings in fixes and security patches from third-party code
is easier in small frequent steps
cards.use: want to avoid falling far behind upstream
not: should be postponed until forced by a vulnerability

cards.subject: Security patching
says: applies fixes for known vulnerabilities
has a target time based on severity
cards.use: learn of a vulnerability in something you run
not: can wait for the next planned feature release

cards.subject: Long-term support
says: promises fixes for a version for an extended period
is chosen when stability matters more than new features
cards.use: run production systems that cannot change often
not: gets all the newest features first

cards.subject: A sunset period
says: is the time between announcing retirement and switching off
gives users time to migrate
cards.use: retire a service people rely on
not: is the period after the service has been turned off

cards.subject: End of life
says: is the point where a product no longer receives fixes
means running it carries growing risk
cards.use: need to plan for the end of a component's support
not: means support continues for security issues only

cards.subject: A migration path
says: gives users a route from the old product to the new one
includes tools, documentation and a timetable
cards.use: retire a product with customers who need a replacement
not: is optional when the replacement is better

cards.subject: Archival at end of life
says: decides what data is kept, for how long and where
is guided by retention duties and privacy law
cards.use: are decommissioning a system that holds records
not: means deleting everything immediately

cards.subject: The bus factor
says: measures how many people can leave before the project stalls
is raised by sharing knowledge
cards.use: worry that one person alone understands the system
not: counts the servers in use

cards.subject: Unsupported software
says: receives no security fixes
becomes a risk that grows over time
cards.use: find a production system running a product past its support date
not: is safe if nothing has gone wrong yet

cards.subject: deploy-check.php
says: is a read-only script that fails if anything would break the app or expose data
is run before and after every upload
cards.use: want a repeatable pre-launch check on ggmoney
not: changes configuration to repair any problem it finds

cards.subject: Running deploy-check.php in a browser
says: tests what Apache actually serves
catches problems a command-line run would not
cards.use: must verify the live web server configuration for ggmoney
not: is unnecessary because the command-line run is identical

cards.subject: The Cloudflare SSL setting for ggmoney
says: is set to Full (strict) before filing
is the one item its guide leaves to do before filing
cards.use: finish the ggmoney launch checklist
not: is left on Flexible because the origin certificate is optional

cards.subject: The HMRC production approvals checklist
says: keeps prepared answers for the approval process
says where an answer would be untrue until something is done
cards.use: prepare ggmoney for HMRC production access
not: contains answers written once and assumed to be true

cards.subject: GGLearn's invite-only sign-up
says: controls who can create an account before wider use
was chosen before the product was opened further
cards.use: launch GGLearn to a limited group
not: lets anyone register with an email address

cards.subject: The GGLearn security review's open items
says: list what remains open, such as Apache restriction to Cloudflare ranges
take effect only once the live vhosts include the restriction
cards.use: look at what GGLearn accepted at launch
not: are all closed before any user is allowed in

cards.subject: ggmoney's docs/hmrc/RUNBOOK.md
says: gives the steps for getting authorised to file with HMRC
is an example of a runbook kept beside the code
cards.use: need instructions for an HMRC authorisation task
not: records the release notes for each version

cards.subject: ggsocial's DEPLOY.md
says: lists traps learned the hard way
notes that the live Apache vhost is a copy and not a symlink
cards.use: deploy ggsocial and want to avoid known mistakes
not: describes the product roadmap

cards.subject: The ggmoney APP_VERSION value
says: is defined in config.php as 0.1.0
is given to HMRC as the software version
cards.use: need the version that appears in an external record
not: is separate from anything sent to HMRC

cards.subject: The ggsocial deployment id
says: is the commit plus a timestamp
makes browsers on an old build reload instead of failing on removed server actions
cards.use: deploy a build that changes server actions
not: is a manually chosen release name

cards.subject: GGLearn's analytics from its own database
says: reads runs, scores and progress already recorded
limits access by role
cards.use: want completion and difficulty trends without a third-party tracker
not: needs an external analytics script on every page

qa.q: What is the main purpose of a go-live checklist?
qa.right: To confirm it is safe to let real users in
wrong: To list every feature that was built
To record who worked on the project
qa.why: A checklist turns 'it works on my machine' into 'safe for real users'.

qa.q: Which part of version 1.4.2 increases for a backward-compatible bug fix?
qa.right: The patch number, giving 1.4.3
qa.why: Under semantic versioning, PATCH is for compatible fixes.

qa.q: Which part of version 1.4.2 increases when you add a backward-compatible feature?
qa.right: The minor number, giving 1.5.0
qa.why: A minor bump resets the patch number to zero.

qa.q: What does a rollback do?
qa.right: Returns the system to the previously released version
wrong: Deploys a new fix on top of the broken release
qa.why: A rollback reverts to the last known good version.

qa.q: What is a runbook?
qa.right: Step-by-step instructions for a known task or incident
wrong: A record of who attended an incident
A forecast of traffic after launch
A list of the features in a release
qa.why: It is written so someone tired can follow it.

qa.q: What does a changelog contain?
qa.right: A list of notable changes per version, written for people
wrong: The source code of each release
qa.why: A changelog is curated, not a raw commit log.

qa.q: Why must a backup be restored at least once before launch?
qa.right: Because only a restore proves the backup is usable
wrong: Because backup tools do not report errors
Because restoring speeds up the next backup
qa.why: An untested backup is an assumption.

qa.q: What is the difference between deploying and releasing when feature flags are used?
qa.right: Deploying puts code on production; releasing exposes the feature to users
wrong: Deploying only happens in test environments
qa.why: Flags separate shipping code from turning behaviour on.

qa.q: What does a status page do during an outage?
qa.right: Shows users the current health of the service so they need not contact support
wrong: Collects bug reports for the next release
Hides the incident until it is resolved
qa.why: It should be hosted separately from the service it reports on.

qa.q: Which statement about a severity level is correct?
qa.right: It sets how urgently an issue must be handled based on impact
wrong: It is chosen by the customer who reports the issue
It describes the age of the bug
It is the same as the priority in the backlog
qa.why: Severity is a pre-agreed classification of impact.

qa.q: What is a good use of first-line support?
qa.right: Answering how-to questions using documentation
qa.why: First line handles known fixes and routes the rest.

qa.q: Why are exit criteria agreed before testing starts?
qa.right: So readiness is judged against an agreed bar rather than argued afterwards
wrong: So defects can be hidden from users
So the release date never changes
qa.why: Criteria fixed up front avoid post-hoc rationalising.

qa.q: What is the aim of hypercare?
qa.right: Extra support in the period straight after launch, with a defined end
wrong: Permanent premium support for large customers
A final round of code review
qa.why: Hypercare is time-boxed intensified support.

qa.q: What should a good analytics event answer?
qa.right: A question decided in advance
wrong: Anything that might be useful someday
Who is the least active user
How many pages the team wrote
qa.why: Track only what answers your questions; every event has a cost.

qa.q: A release notes entry should be written in whose language?
qa.right: The users'
qa.why: Say what changed, why it matters and what people must do.

qa.q: A team ships a release with a migration that drops a column. The release then fails. Why may a rollback not be enough?
qa.right: Reverting the code does not restore the dropped data
wrong: Rollbacks always require a new build
The old code never reads that column
qa.why: Destructive migrations create a point of no return.

qa.q: Which strategy sends a small share of real traffic to a new version and compares it with the old?
qa.right: Canary release
qa.why: A canary checks health on a small audience before widening.

qa.q: Which strategy keeps two full production environments and switches traffic between them?
qa.right: Blue-green deployment
qa.why: Rollback becomes switching traffic back.

qa.q: What makes an expand-contract migration rollback-safe?
qa.right: The old schema stays until no code uses it
wrong: The old column is dropped first
Data is copied to a spreadsheet
The migration runs only on weekends
qa.why: Old and new code can run against the same database during the transition.

qa.q: Why is a response target not the same as a resolution target?
qa.right: A response target measures time to a first meaningful reply, not time to fix
wrong: A response target only applies to outages
A resolution target is always shorter
They are the same measure in different units
qa.why: You can meet a response target while a problem takes days.

qa.q: Why does p99 latency matter more than average latency for spotting bad experiences?
qa.right: The average hides the slowest requests
wrong: The average is more expensive to compute
qa.why: Percentiles show tail latency users actually feel.

qa.q: What is the difference between an SLI and an SLO?
qa.right: The SLI is the measurement; the SLO is the target for it
wrong: The SLI is the contract; the SLO is the dashboard
The SLO is measured by customers; the SLI by engineers
qa.why: An indicator is measured and an objective sets the goal.

qa.q: What does synthetic monitoring detect that real user monitoring may not?
qa.right: A key journey failing when no real users are present
wrong: How different devices render a page
Which countries have the most users
The size of a user's screen
qa.why: Scripted checks run on a schedule regardless of traffic.

qa.q: A dashboard shows sign-ups doubling after a campaign, but retention stays flat. What does that suggest?
qa.right: Sign-ups alone may be a vanity metric and value is not improving
wrong: The product is performing twice as well
The campaign should be repeated unchanged
qa.why: Retention and activation show whether users find value.

qa.q: Which maintenance type changes software to cope with a new platform version?
qa.right: Adaptive
qa.why: Adaptive maintenance responds to environment change.

qa.q: Which maintenance type restructures code to lower the risk of future faults?
qa.right: Preventive
qa.why: Preventive work reduces future problems before they appear.

qa.q: What is the purpose of a lockfile?
qa.right: To record exact dependency versions so builds are repeatable
wrong: To prevent anyone editing the code
qa.why: It makes each install use the same versions.

qa.q: What does a blameless post-incident review ask?
qa.right: How the system and process allowed the failure
wrong: How the incident can be hidden
qa.why: Blame discourages honest accounts and hides learning.

qa.q: What is a good outcome of a retrospective?
qa.right: A few agreed actions, each with an owner and a date
wrong: A long list of everything that went wrong
A statement that everyone will try harder
A ranked list of team members
qa.why: Actions without owners rarely happen.

qa.q: Which handover step lets the receiving team operate while the builders watch?
qa.right: Reverse shadowing
qa.why: It confirms the receivers can run the system unaided.

qa.q: A team has a green checklist but one item, rate limiting, is not in place. What is the best approach?
qa.right: Record it in the known-gap register with an owner and a date, and decide on purpose whether to launch
wrong: Mark the item done to keep the checklist green
qa.why: Accepted gaps should be visible and owned.

qa.q: An on-call engineer is paged six times a night, mostly by alerts needing no action. What should the team do first?
qa.right: Remove or retune alerts that need no action and page on user-visible symptoms
wrong: Rotate on-call less often so people tolerate it
qa.why: Alert fatigue hides the alerts that matter.

qa.q: Your error budget for the quarter is spent in week three. What does the policy usually imply?
qa.right: Prioritise reliability work and slow risky releases until budget returns
wrong: Release faster to recover the lost time
Raise the objective to look better
Ignore the budget until the quarter ends
qa.why: The budget guides how much change risk is acceptable.

qa.q: After a redesign, sign-ups jump 30 percent in week one and then settle back. What is the likeliest explanation?
qa.right: A novelty effect
wrong: The redesign is clearly permanent success
qa.why: Early excitement fades; judge a change over a longer period.

qa.q: A team wants to test a new checkout and needs to avoid harming speed or error rates. What should be added?
qa.right: Guardrail metrics
qa.why: Guardrails catch harm while another metric is optimised.

qa.q: A feature has been deprecated. What is the minimum that users need?
qa.right: A stated removal date, a replacement and a migration route
wrong: A notice on the day it is removed
A promise that nothing will change
Only an update to the changelog
qa.why: Depending users need time and a path.

qa.q: A team deploys a new server component and wants real load tested without showing users results. Which approach fits?
qa.right: Dark launch
qa.why: A dark launch exercises code on live traffic invisibly.

qa.q: The service owner leaves and nobody knows how to restore the system. Which metric was ignored?
qa.right: The bus factor
qa.why: Knowledge held by one person is a risk.

qa.q: A product is retired and holds customer records. What should be decided before switching it off?
qa.right: What data to keep, for how long and where, based on retention duties
wrong: Nothing, because deleted data cannot cause problems
Only which servers to power off
How to announce the shutdown on social media
qa.why: Archival and deletion must follow retention and privacy rules.

qa.q: Support receives the same question every week. Which action best uses this as feedback?
qa.right: Fix the cause in the product or documentation and add a knowledge base article
wrong: Ask users to read more carefully
Close the tickets with a standard reply
qa.why: Patterns in questions point to unclear product or docs.

qa.q: A hypercare period has ended by the calendar, but high-severity issues remain open and metrics are unstable. What should the team do?
qa.right: Extend hypercare because exit criteria are not met
wrong: Move all issues to the backlog without review
Hide the issues from the status report
qa.why: Exit should depend on criteria, not only dates.

qa.q: A team runs a canary at 5 percent and sees the error rate unchanged, but latency for one customer segment doubles. What is the best next step?
qa.right: Hold the rollout and investigate that segment before widening
wrong: Widen to 100 percent because errors are flat
Roll back to the oldest version available
qa.why: Aggregates can hide a harmful segment effect.

qa.q: An incident review concludes the cause was 'human error'. What is the best response?
qa.right: Ask what in the system made the error likely and add safeguards
wrong: Accept the conclusion and close the review
qa.why: Human error is a starting point, not a cause.

qa.q: A release needs a non-reversible database change. What should be decided before go-live?
qa.right: Who accepts the point of no return, and what the roll-forward plan is
wrong: Nothing, since rollback will cover it
Whether to hide the change from support
Which day of the week it runs
qa.why: A point of no return is a deliberate decision.

qa.q: A dependency has gone without updates for two years and now has a known vulnerability. What is the first thing to establish?
qa.right: Whether the dependency is still supported and what migration options exist
wrong: Whether the vulnerability is old enough to ignore
qa.why: Unsupported software carries growing risk and needs a migration path.

qa.q: A team has an A/B test running for one day showing a 3 percent lift. What is the main concern?
qa.right: Too little time and data to separate the effect from noise
wrong: The lift is too small to matter
The control group is too large
qa.why: Short tests mislead through noise and novelty.

qa.q: A team is in the middle of an outage and users keep asking for news. What helps most?
qa.right: Posting updates at a promised cadence even when there is nothing new
wrong: Waiting until the root cause is known
Replying only to the largest customers
qa.why: A cadence reduces repeat questions and builds trust.

qa.q: Which item belongs in a handover pack?
qa.right: Documentation, access, contacts and known issues
wrong: A list of who to blame for defects
qa.why: The receiver needs what is required to operate the system.

qa.q: A team wants release notes and versions generated from history. Which practice enables it?
qa.right: Conventional commit messages
qa.why: Typed commit prefixes drive version bumps and changelog entries.

qa.q: For ggmoney, what does deploy-check.php do?
qa.right: Fails if anything would break the app or expose data, without changing anything
qa.why: It is a read-only pre- and post-upload check.

qa.q: Why is deploy-check.php run in a browser as well as on the command line?
qa.right: A browser run tests what Apache actually serves
wrong: The command line cannot run PHP
qa.why: Web server behaviour differs from the CLI.

qa.q: What does the ggsocial deployment id (commit plus timestamp) prevent?
qa.right: Old browser builds failing when they call server actions that no longer exist
qa.why: Browsers on an old build reload instead of failing.

qa.q: Why is ggmoney's APP_VERSION of 0.1.0 important to keep consistent?
qa.right: The same value is given to HMRC as the software version
wrong: It sets the Cloudflare SSL mode
qa.why: It forms part of an external record.

qa.q: What did GGLearn do about sign-up before wider use?
qa.right: Made sign-up invite-only
wrong: Moved sign-up to a third-party service
qa.why: Controlled sign-up limits who can enter at launch.

qa.q: The GGLearn security review lists Apache restriction to Cloudflare ranges as open. When does it take effect?
qa.right: Once the live vhosts include the restriction
wrong: As soon as the review is written
qa.why: The config exists but must be included in the live vhosts.

qa.q: Why does ggsocial's DEPLOY.md note that the live Apache vhost is a copy and not a symlink?
qa.right: Edits to the repo file do not change the live vhost until it is copied
qa.why: A known trap listed in the deploy guide.

qa.q: What should the Cloudflare SSL mode for ggmoney be set to before filing?
qa.right: Full (strict)
qa.why: The guide leaves this as the one item to do before filing.

qa.q: The HMRC production approvals checklist 'says where an answer would be untrue until something is done'. Why is that useful?
qa.right: It stops anyone submitting an answer that is false at the time of submission
wrong: It lets answers be changed after approval
It replaces the need to do the work
qa.why: Honest answers depend on the underlying work being finished.

qa.q: How can GGLearn read completion and difficulty trends without a third-party tracker?
qa.right: From runs, scores and progress already stored in its database, limited by role
qa.why: First-party data may suffice.
